4. Upon the aforesaid pleadings certain issues were framed and evidence was led by the parties in respect of their respective contentions. The High court on a consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case and evidence on record came to the finding that defendant Nos. 2 and 3 had been possessing the disputed land since 1946 as tenants and thereafter as purchasers on the basis of purchase from defendant No. 1 in 1949 and that they been possessing the disputed land since 1949 by virtue of the right acquired by them by making improvements of, and construction on the suit land. The learned Subordinate Judge however held that defendant No. 1 had contracted to sell and thereafter sold the land in 1949 to the defendant Nos. 2 and 1 for valuable consideration. On the question whether the patta marked Ext. C. executed by defendant No. 1 in favour of defendant Nos 2 and 3 and the kabala marked Ext. D executed by defendant No.1 in favour of the wives of defendant Nos. 2 and 3 constituted a single transaction amounting to a sale of he disputed land, was placed on of the contesting defendants in the trial court upon the decision reported in Md. Hossain Mia Vs. Member, Board of Revenue, 14 D.L R Dacca. page 87 in which it was held that a deed of lease followed immediately by a deed of sale of the rent-receiving interest of the lease hold property in favour of the same person constituted a transaction of out and our sale of the property But the learned Subordinate Judge appears to have distinguished the said case on the ground that in the instant case the kabala Ext. D was not in favour of defendant Nos. 2 and 3, the repents of the Patta, Ext. C but in favour of their and as such was of the opinion that the deed of lease, Ext. C and the kabala, Ext. D did not constitute a single transaction of sale, but were two separate transaction. On that view of the matter the deed of lease, Ext C executed by defendant No 1 in favour of defendant Nos. 2 and 3 was held to have been hit by section 9 and section 75A of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, and as such was null and void in the eye of law The learned Subordinate Judge however, held that defendant Nos. 2 and 3 acquired good title to the disputed land on the basis of continuous possession of the same for more than 12 years. He came to further findings that defendant No. 1 was in charge of the prosecution of the suit on behalf of the plaintiff and that the bainanama, Ext. 1 purported to be executed by defendant No. 1 in favour of the plaintiff was a collusive document, the suit was dismissed on the basis of the aforesaid findings. 

 5. The plaintiff preferred an appeal against the decision of the learned Subordinate Judge, which being heard by the Court of the Additional District Judge, Chittagong was allowed and the suit was decreed declaring the plaintiff's title to the disputed land and also decreeing recovery for Khas possession of the disputed land by evicting defendant No. 2 and 3 therefrom. In course of the Judgment, the learned Additional District Judge came to the findings that the story of tenancy in respect of the disputed land since 1940 as set up by defendant Nos. 2 and 3 was a mere concoction that there was no contract to sell in favour of defendant Nos. 2 and 3 in respect of the disputed land in 1949 nor any earnest money was paid in pursuance of the said contract, that the contesting defendants had been in possession of the disputed land since 1956-57 and that the suit being filed in 1961, mere was no acquisition of valid title by adverse possession. As regards the legal effect of the lease Ext. C and the kabala, Ext. D the learned Additional District Judge appears to be of the view, concurrently with the learned Subordinate Judge, that the deed of lease Ext C was void in view of section 9 and section 75A of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the kabala, Ext. D, by which the rent-receiving interest was purported to have been transferred was also void in inasmuch as no private person could sell the rent-receiving-interest after the 14th April, 1956. 

 13. We have, therefore, no hesitation in ho ding that these two documents together constitute one and single transaction of out and oat sale and bosh the courts how committed an error of law in construing the said and in considering the said transaction essentially to be a lease which being hit by sections 9 and 75A of the East Bengal state Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 was null and void In the said event defendant Nos 2 and 3 acquired good title in the disputed land by purchase on 15-4-57.
